newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan steelmakers see benefits in Hanbo strife.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan steelmakers see benefits in Hanbo strife.

text.p: Taiwan steelmakers expect to benefit from a financial crisis at South Korea's Hanbo Steel Co Ltd that comes at a time of national labour strife, executives and analysts said on Monday.
"Hanbo's financial problems and the South Korean workers' strikes will push some orders to other Asian countries," said an official of top Taiwan maker China Steel Corp.
Taiwan will be seen as an attractive alternative for such rerouted orders, he said.
Hanbo Steel, a unit of the giant Hanbo Group, said on Friday it was filing for court receivership after failing to honour payments of more than five billion won (US$5.8 million).
Taiwan industry analysts said Asian steel prices could rise as Hanbo Steel's plan to build a major steel mill was likely to be delayed or diminished.
"Hanbo plans to build new plants this year to add another 350 million tonnes' production, but the company is unlikely to meet that target now," the China Steel official said.
Hanbo already had capacity of 350 million tonnes a year but produced only 300 million tonnes, he said.
Taiwan traders said regional prices for hot-rolled steel coil, Hanbo's main product, would benefit the most.

Taiwan analysts said Hanbo's crisis seemed to result from its rapid investment in a shift to expensive new production methods, including building more electric-powered furnaces and two milling plants using a method called COREX.

They said electric-powered furnaces, while cheaper to run, were not competitive with traditional blast furnaces in production quality and that COREX plants required huge amounts of up-front capital investment.
Taiwan's Yieh Loong Co had evaluated use of COREX but backed away after learning of its intensive capital requirements, Yieh Loong president Kuo Yen-tu told Reuters.
"Our evaluation shows the COREX process is too costly and not suitable for us," Kuo said.
COREX plants required more land and additional capital for sideline-power generating plants and oxygen generators, Kuo said.
Kuo declined to discuss specific costs of COREX plants but said they were much higher than expected. "COREX requires much more capital than we expected," he said.
South Korea's finance ministry said Hanbo was saddled with about five trillion won in debt against its net worth of 224.3 billion won (US$265 million).
South Korean analysts said Hanbo's plant under construction at Tangjin had so far cost 4.96 trillion won and needed 750 billion won more to complete.
They said Hanbo Steel seemed to be on the brink of collapse. The steelmaker is the flagship of Hanbo Group, South Korea's 14th-largest conglomerate.
South Korean President Kim Young-sam ordered a probe into the conglomerate while opposition parties alleged government complicity in what they called irregular loans to Hanbo Steel.
